title: Your Grandmother's Eyes
principle: Someone who carries a broken copy without showing it is called a carrier.

t: Something skips a generation. Your grandmother had it, your mother did not, you do.
A trait appears, vanishes for a generation, and comes back. Nothing was lost and nothing was regained — and that pattern is a fingerprint.
sub: How can it disappear and then come back?
The way a trait moves through a family tells you what kind of trait it is, before you sequence anything.

question: How can something skip a whole generation?
What must be true for a trait to skip a generation entirely?
options: It was passed on by someone else
note: Guess first — you already know enough to work this out.
Commit. The previous lesson has already given you everything needed.

t: Match each family pattern to what it tells you.
Each pattern of inheritance leaves a distinctive signature in a family tree. Match them.

label: Skips generations; parents unaffected
Appears in siblings with unaffected parents; both sexes equally
Shows in every generation
Present in every generation, affected child always has an affected parent
Mostly boys, passed through mothers
Predominantly males, transmitted through unaffected female carriers, never father to son

t: Someone who carries a broken copy without showing it is called a carrier.
A person with one broken copy and no signs of the condition is a carrier — and most people are carriers of something.
Heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic for recessive conditions. The average person carries several severe recessive alleles without knowing.

Every person carries an estimated one to two alleles that would be lethal or severely disabling in the homozygous state. This is the actual basis of the harm from close-relative marriage: shared ancestry raises the chance that both parents carry the same rare allele.
sub: Which is why it can hide for a generation and then show up.
The trait did not skip anything. It was present the whole time, just not visible.
'Skipping a generation' is a description of the phenotype, never of the genotype — the allele was transmitted every step of the way.
The distinction matters for reasoning about family history: absence of the phenotype in a generation is weak evidence about the genotype, and pedigrees are read with that asymmetry in mind.

q: Did the trait really skip a generation?
In what sense did the trait skip a generation?
Is 'skipping a generation' an accurate description?
options: No — the instruction was there, it just did not show
Yes, it was gone and came back
Yes, it jumped from grandmother to grandchild directly
why: Your mother had the broken copy and passed it to you. She had a working copy too, so it never showed in her.
The allele was transmitted at every step. Only the phenotype was absent, because the intervening carrier also had a working copy. Nothing skipped anything.

Genotype and phenotype come apart here, which is precisely why the distinction is worth having. Nothing can jump a generation — transmission is strictly stepwise — so any apparent skip is an unexpressed carrier.

q: Why can a family tree tell you the pattern before any test?
What licenses inferring a mode of inheritance from a pedigree alone?
options: Because each pattern forbids things the others allow
Because affected people always look alike
Because the traits are always visible
why: Each pattern rules something out. X-linked recessive never goes father to son — so a single father-to-son transmission kills that explanation on its own, whatever else the tree looks like.

Pedigree analysis works by exclusion rather than accumulation. Each mode forbids particular transmissions — no male-to-male transmission for X-linked, no unaffected parent of an affected child for a fully penetrant dominant — so a single observation in the forbidden class eliminates a hypothesis outright. It is the same forbidden-outcome logic you met in the evidence lesson, applied to families.

t: Drawing a family tree is still one of the first things a doctor does.

A three-generation pedigree costs nothing, takes ten minutes, and remains one of the highest-yield tools in clinical genetics — it often narrows the possibilities enough to choose which test to order, or to show that no test is warranted.
